logicalDeduction.name: Logical Deduction
logicalDeduction.tagline: Use the clues to work out who has what.
logicalDeduction.description: Each person has exactly one item from every list, and no two people share an item. Read the clues, rule out what cannot be true, and answer one question. Higher levels add people, more lists to match and clues that only say what is not true.
logicalDeduction.scoringSummary: Each puzzle has exactly one answer. Your result is the share of puzzles answered correctly; there is no time limit.

instructions.items: Each person has exactly one item from each list, and no two people have the same item.
instructions.clues: Read every clue. Clues are always true.
instructions.ruleOut: Rule out what cannot be true until only one answer is left, then answer the question.
instructions.tip: Tip: “not” clues are useful — if someone does not have two of three items, they have the third.

logicalDeduction.simpleInstructions: Read the clues and find out who has what.

levels.1: Three people, one list, simple clues.
levels.2: Three people, one list, “not” and “either” clues.
levels.4: Match two lists for three people.
levels.6: Two lists for four people, linked clues.
levels.7: Two lists for four people with no direct answers.
levels.10: Five people, two lists, only indirect clues.

logicalDeduction.explanation_one: Only one way to share out the items fits the clue: {{rows}}. Every other way breaks it. So {{fact}}
logicalDeduction.explanation_other: Only one way to share out the items fits all {{count}} clues: {{rows}}. Every other way breaks at least one clue. So {{fact}}

shared.cluesTitle: Clues · all of them are true

numberSequences.name: Number Sequences
numberSequences.tagline: Find the rule, then the number.
numberSequences.description: A row of numbers follows a hidden rule. Work out the rule and type the next number, or the one that is missing. Higher levels use rules that alternate, grow, or mix two sequences together.
numberSequences.scoringSummary: Each sequence has one answer that every simple rule agrees on. Your result is the share of numbers typed exactly right; there is no time limit.
numberSequences.simpleInstructions: Find the pattern and type the missing number.

instructions.1: Look at how each number changes into the next one.
instructions.2: Try simple rules first: adding, subtracting, multiplying.
instructions.3: If the change is not the same each time, look at how the changes themselves change, or at every second number.
instructions.4: Type the number that replaces the question mark.

levels.1: Add the same small number each time.
levels.2: Steps that go up or down.
levels.4: Find a missing number in the middle.
levels.9: Each number built from the two before it.
levels.10: Any rule, often with a gap in the middle.

prompt.missing: Which number replaces the question mark?

numberSequences.explanation: The rule is: {{rule}}. That gives {{shown}}, so the answer is {{answer}}. No other simple rule fits all the numbers shown.

rule.growing: the amount added grows by {{dd}} each time (add {{a}}, then {{b}}, then {{c}}, …)
rule.interleaved: two sequences take turns: the 1st, 3rd, 5th … terms {{a}} each time, and the 2nd, 4th, 6th … terms {{b}} each time
rule.sumOfTwo: each term is the sum of the two terms before it

ruleDiscovery.name: Rule Discovery
ruleDiscovery.tagline: Spot the hidden rule from examples.
ruleDiscovery.description: Some items fit a secret rule and some do not. Compare the two groups, work out the rule, and choose the new item that fits it. Higher levels use rules with “not”, “or” and “and”, and give fewer examples.
ruleDiscovery.scoringSummary: Exactly one option fits every rule that matches the examples. Your result is the share of puzzles answered correctly; there is no time limit.
ruleDiscovery.simpleInstructions: Find what the “yes” items share and pick the new one that matches.

instructions.1: The items under “Fits the rule” all follow one secret rule. The items under “Does not fit” break it.
instructions.2: Look for what every item that fits has in common — and what the others lack.
instructions.3: Then choose the one option that fits the same rule.
instructions.4: Shapes are named by colour and shape, so you never need to tell colours apart by sight alone.

levels.2: Colour or shape: which one matters?
levels.3: Rules about numbers: even, odd, big or small.
levels.4: Rules that say what something is not.
levels.6: “Or” rules: one of two features is enough.
levels.7: Shapes and numbers, every simple rule.
levels.8: “And” rules: two things must both be true.
levels.10: Any rule, more options to check.

ruleDiscovery.explanation_one: The rule is: {{rule}}. The answer, {{answer}}, fits it; {{wrong}} does not. Every other simple rule either breaks one of the examples or picks the same answer.
ruleDiscovery.explanation_other: The rule is: {{rule}}. The answer, {{answer}}, fits it; {{wrong}} do not. Every other simple rule either breaks one of the examples or picks the same answer.

rule.colorOrShape: the shape is $t(kit:color.{{color}}), or it is $t(logic:ruleDiscovery.aShape.{{shape}}) (or both)

conditionalReasoning.name: Conditional Reasoning
conditionalReasoning.tagline: If this, then that — what really follows?
conditionalReasoning.description: Read a few “if … then …” statements and facts, then decide whether a sentence must be true, must be false, or cannot be decided. Higher levels chain rules together and use “unless” and “only if”.
conditionalReasoning.scoringSummary: Each answer is checked against every situation that fits the statements. Your result is the share of answers that are correct; there is no time limit.
conditionalReasoning.simpleInstructions: Use only the rules to decide: yes for sure, no for sure, or can’t tell.

instructions.1: Treat every statement as true, even if it sounds unusual.
instructions.2: Use only what the statements say — nothing else.
instructions.3: “Must be true” or “must be false” means no other situation is possible. Otherwise choose “Can’t tell”.
instructions.4: Careful: “if A, then B” does not mean “if B, then A”.

levels.1: One rule, and its “if” part is true.
levels.2: Work backwards: the result did not happen.
levels.3: Spot the traps where you can’t tell.
levels.5: Chains: two rules in a row.
levels.10: Several mixed rules about four things.

notes.affirm-antecedent: The rule applies, because its “if” part is true, so its “then” part follows.
notes.deny-consequent: If the “if” part were true, the “then” part would be true too — but it is not, so the “if” part cannot be true.
notes.affirm-consequent: Knowing the “then” part is a common trap: it could be true for some other reason, so the “if” part is not settled.
notes.deny-antecedent: The rule only says what happens when its “if” part is true. Here it is not, so the rule tells us nothing.
notes.unless: “X unless Y” means: if Y is not true, then X is true.
notes.onlyIf: “X only if Y” means: if X is true, then Y is true.

view.title: Statements · treat them all as true

because.true: Every situation that fits all the statements has “$t(logic:conditionalReasoning.atoms.{{a}}.main)” true, so it must be true.
because.false: Every situation that fits all the statements has “$t(logic:conditionalReasoning.atoms.{{a}}.main)” false, so it must be false.
because.unknown: Both are possible: “$t(logic:conditionalReasoning.atoms.{{a}}.main)” is true if {{yes}}, and false if {{no}}. So you can't tell.

constraintSolver.name: Constraint Solver
constraintSolver.tagline: Fill the grid in your head and find one number.
constraintSolver.description: Each row and each column holds every number once. Use the numbers already given — and, at higher levels, boxes and “smaller than” signs — to work out the number in the highlighted cell.
constraintSolver.scoringSummary: Each grid has exactly one solution. Your result is the share of highlighted cells you work out correctly; there is no time limit.
constraintSolver.simpleInstructions: No number twice in a row or column — find the missing one.

instructions.1: Every row and every column must contain each number exactly once.
instructions.2: When boxes are drawn, each box must also contain each number once.
instructions.3: A clue like “A1 < B1” means the number in A1 is smaller than the number in B1.
instructions.4: Type the number that belongs in the highlighted cell (marked “?”).

levels.1: A 3×3 grid with most numbers given.
levels.9: A 6×6 grid with boxes and few numbers.
levels.10: A 6×6 grid with boxes and “smaller than” clues.

explanation.plain: The grid has only one solution that keeps every rule. In it, row {{row}} reads {{values}}, so {{cell}} is {{answer}}.
explanation.inequalities: The grid has only one solution that keeps every rule, including the “smaller than” clues. In it, row {{row}} reads {{values}}, so {{cell}} is {{answer}}.

view.rowsRule: Each row and each column holds 1 to {{size}} once.
view.boxRule: Each {{h}}×{{w}} box (thick borders) also holds 1 to {{size}} once.

sequenceOrdering.name: Sequence Ordering
sequenceOrdering.tagline: Put everyone in the right order.
sequenceOrdering.description: Use clues such as “Ana finished ahead of Ben” or “exactly one person stands between them” to work out the full order. Higher levels add people and clues that only rule things out.
sequenceOrdering.scoringSummary: Exactly one order fits all the clues. An answer counts when every position is right. Your result is the share of puzzles ordered correctly; there is no time limit.
sequenceOrdering.simpleInstructions: Use the clues to put the names in order.

instructions.1: Read every clue. Exactly one order fits all of them.
instructions.2: Start with clues that fix a position (“first”, “last”), then place the others around them.
instructions.3: Use the arrow buttons to move names up or down, then submit your order.

levels.1: Order three people with simple clues.
levels.4: Four people, clues about who is not where.

prompt.race: Put the runners in finishing order, first at the top.
prompt.queue: Put the people in line order, front of the line at the top.

sequenceOrdering.explanation_one: Only one order fits the clue: {{order}}. Check the clue against it; moving anyone breaks it.
sequenceOrdering.explanation_other: Only one order fits all {{count}} clues: {{order}}. Check each clue against it; moving anyone breaks at least one clue.

queue.nextTo: {{a}} and {{b}} stand next to each other.

truthAndFalsehood.name: Truth and Falsehood
truthAndFalsehood.tagline: Some always tell the truth, some always lie.
truthAndFalsehood.description: Each character is either a truth-teller, who only says true things, or a liar, who only says false things. Test each possibility against what they say to find the only one that works. Higher levels add characters and statements about the whole group.
truthAndFalsehood.scoringSummary: Exactly one way of sorting truth-tellers and liars fits what everyone says. Your result is the share of puzzles answered correctly; there is no time limit.
truthAndFalsehood.simpleInstructions: Truth-tellers never lie, liars never tell the truth — find out who is who.

instructions.1: A truth-teller only says true things. A liar only says false things.
instructions.2: Pick one character and suppose they tell the truth. Does everything else still fit? If not, they must be lying.
instructions.3: Exactly one way of sorting everyone works. Use it to answer the question.

levels.1: Two characters talk about each other.
levels.2: Two characters: “we are the same” or “different”.
levels.6: Three characters, every kind of statement.
levels.8: Four characters, “at least one of” statements.
levels.10: Four characters, every kind of statement.

different.withMe: {{other}} and I are different: one truth-teller and one liar

honest.withMe: At least one of {{other}} and me is a truth-teller

liar.pair: At least one of {{a}} and {{b}} is a liar
liar.withMe: At least one of {{other}} and me is a liar

exactly.liar_one: Exactly one of us is a liar

strategyPuzzle.name: Strategy Puzzle
strategyPuzzle.tagline: Plan ahead: find the best move or the shortest way.
strategyPuzzle.description: Coin games where you must find the move that guarantees a win, water jugs to measure an exact amount, and sliding tiles to put back in place. Every answer is checked by searching all possibilities, so the best move or the smallest number of moves is certain.
strategyPuzzle.scoringSummary: Answers are checked against an exhaustive search. Your result is the share of puzzles answered correctly; there is no time limit.

instructions.1: Coin games: you and a friend take turns. Whoever takes the last coin wins. Your friend always plays the best move.
instructions.2: Water jugs: fill a jug from the tap, empty it, or pour one jug into another until it is full or the first is empty. Each counts as one move.
instructions.3: Sliding tiles: slide a tile next to the gap into the gap. Each slide counts as one move.
instructions.4: Plan in your head, then answer. Use paper if it helps.

strategyPuzzle.simpleInstructions: Think a few moves ahead to find the best move or the fewest moves.

levels.1: Take 1 or 2 coins: find the winning move.
levels.2: Slide tiles on a small board.
levels.4: Take 1 to 3 coins from a bigger pile.
levels.9: Three jugs and no tap: pour only.
levels.10: Three piles, long slides and three jugs.

prompt.takeAway_other: It is your turn. There are {{count}} coins. Which move makes sure you take the last coin?

prompt.jugs_other: What is the smallest number of moves to get exactly {{count}} litres in one jug?

explanation.takeAway: Take {{take}}, leaving {{left}}. Positions with {{losing}} coins lose for the player whose turn it is: whatever your friend takes (1 to {{max}}), you take the rest of {{group}} and reach the next one, until you take the last coin. Any other move leaves a number your friend can use the same way.
explanation.piles: {{move}}, leaving piles of {{after}}. Checking every possible game from there, each reply your friend makes leaves you a move that keeps you winning, until you take the last coin. Every other move gives your friend such a winning reply.
explanation.pilesEqual: {{move}}, leaving piles of {{after}}. Checking every possible game from there, each reply your friend makes leaves you a move that keeps you winning, until you take the last coin. With two equal piles, you can copy every move your friend makes on the other pile. Every other move gives your friend such a winning reply.

algorithmicReasoning.name: Algorithmic Reasoning
algorithmicReasoning.tagline: Follow the robot’s instructions step by step.
algorithmicReasoning.description: A robot follows a list of plain instructions: move forward, turn, do something several times, or check for a wall. Follow it in your head and point to the square where it stops. Higher levels add repeats, repeats inside repeats and checks for walls.
algorithmicReasoning.scoringSummary: The robot’s path is simulated exactly. Your result is the share of end squares found correctly; there is no time limit.
algorithmicReasoning.accessibilityNotes: Each square is named by row and column, and the robot’s start and direction are spoken, so the path can be followed without seeing the grid.
algorithmicReasoning.simpleInstructions: Follow the arrows in your head and tap where the robot ends up.

instructions.1: The arrow shows where the robot starts and which way it faces.
instructions.2: “Turn left” and “turn right” change the direction it faces; they do not move it.
instructions.3: Walls (striped squares) and the edge block the way. The robot never walks into them.
instructions.4: Follow every instruction in order, then press the square where the robot stops.

levels.1: Move and turn on a small grid.
levels.2: A few more steps, and walls.
levels.3: Do the same thing several times.
levels.4: Keep going until something blocks the way.
levels.5: Check for a wall before moving.

program.ifBlocked: If the square in front is a wall or the edge:
program.untilBlocked: Keep moving forward until the square in front is a wall or the edge.

algorithmicReasoning.prompt: Where does the robot stop? Press that square.
algorithmicReasoning.explanation: The robot starts at {{start}} facing {{facing}}. Then: {{steps}}. It stops at {{end}}.

multiStepLogic.name: Multi-Step Logic Challenge
multiStepLogic.tagline: Chain several facts together to reach the answer.
multiStepLogic.description: Facts link people together: who is older, who has more, who is taller. No single fact gives the answer — you must combine them step by step. Higher levels add people, “twice as many” and totals, and mix numbers with comparisons.
multiStepLogic.scoringSummary: Every answer is checked by trying all possible numbers or orders. Your result is the share of answers that are correct; there is no time limit.
multiStepLogic.simpleInstructions: Put the facts together, one at a time, to find the answer.

instructions.1: Every fact is true. No single fact gives the answer on its own.
instructions.2: Start from what you know for sure (a known age or a total) and work outwards one fact at a time.
instructions.3: “Twice as many” means double; “half as many” means divide by two.
instructions.4: Some questions ask for a number, others ask for a name.

levels.1: One step: from a known number to the next.
levels.3: Who is tallest? Chain the comparisons.
levels.6: Use a total instead of a known number.
levels.7: Differences between people never compared directly.
levels.10: Five people, every kind of fact.
